summary: Gives a new, accurate definition of DNS zone transfer (AXFR), one of the ways authoritative name servers keep their zone data in sync. The older definition in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 lacked detail, so this records how interoperable implementations actually behave. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC specifies how a DNS server sends a complete copy of a zone to another server. It defines the query, response sequence, TCP behavior, and checks that keep an incomplete transfer from replacing valid zone data.

what does the soa record do in axfr
subtitle: How DNS transfers a complete zone over TCP, including the framing and integrity rules clients must follow.

tldr.problem: The original AXFR description was spread across two RFCs and lacked enough detail for interoperable implementations.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends an AXFR query over TCP. The server returns the zone records in one or more messages, starting and ending with the same SOA record.
tldr.outcome: The RFC records interoperable AXFR behavior and updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035. RFC 5936 is updated by RFC 9103.

today: RFC 5936 is a Proposed Standard, published in June 2010. It updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and is updated by RFC 9103.

sections.title: Why AXFR Needed a Precise Definition
sections.content:
DNS has three protocol mechanisms for keeping authoritative servers coherent: AXFR for full zone transfer, IXFR for incremental transfer, and NOTIFY for prompt notice of changes. Earlier AXFR rules appeared in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 but did not specify enough detail for implementations to interoperate without assumptions.

RFC 5936 records an accurate description of the interoperable AXFR behavior. It covers AXFR only; IXFR and NOTIFY remain outside its scope. A DNS implementation is not required to support AXFR.
sections.plainLanguage: AXFR copies a complete DNS zone between servers. This RFC writes down the rules needed for different implementations to exchange that copy consistently.

sections.title: The AXFR Query
sections.content:
An AXFR session begins with one DNS query from the AXFR client. The query has one Question naming the zone, uses QTYPE AXFR (252), and specifies the zone's class. Its Answer and Authority sections MUST be empty.

The query's header uses QR 0, OPCODE 0, and RCODE 0. The client chooses an ID that is not already in use with that server. The Additional section may include an EDNS OPT record and a transaction-security record such as TSIG or SIG(0).
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends one standard DNS query that names the zone and requests AXFR. Optional records can provide EDNS or transaction security information.

sections.title: The AXFR Response Sequence
sections.content:
A successful response contains one or more DNS messages. The first message begins with the zone's SOA record, and the last ends with the same SOA record. Intermediate messages MUST NOT contain that SOA record. Records other than the opening and closing SOA can appear in any order, and clients MUST ignore duplicates.

The server copies the query's Question into the first response. It copies the query ID into every response, sets QR to 1, and does not set the truncation bit. A message can be up to 65535 octets under the TCP length prefix. An error response ends the session and does not need a closing SOA.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends the zone in one or more messages, with the same SOA record marking the beginning and end. Clients accept other records in any order and ignore duplicates.

sections.title: Which Zone Records Are Transferred
sections.content:
The transfer must let the client reconstruct the zone as served by the primary server for the given serial number. The response includes the records registered with that zone, including delegation NS records and the applicable glue records, even when they differ from authoritative data elsewhere.

Keeping a zone and serial number associated with one consistent record set matters when a client later applies an incremental transfer. Occluded names beneath a delegation or DNAME are also included so an administrator can recover them if an update was made in error.
sections.plainLanguage: The transfer reproduces the zone's served contents, including delegation data and names hidden below a delegation. That gives the receiving server a consistent copy for later updates.

sections.title: TCP Connections and Session Handling
sections.content:
AXFR uses TCP; AXFR over UDP is not defined. A TCP connection can carry an AXFR session along with other DNS queries, and it can carry multiple transfers at once. Servers MUST handle multiple AXFR sessions on one connection.

A client cancels a transfer by closing the connection, which also cancels other activity using that connection. If the connection closes remotely, the client cancels its outstanding sessions and should avoid repeated retries that continue indefinitely or increase in frequency. Reusing an open connection is recommended when it works reliably.
sections.plainLanguage: AXFR uses a reliable TCP connection and can share that connection with other DNS activity. Closing it cancels every session using it, not just one transfer.

sections.title: Authorization, Zone Integrity, and Security
sections.content:
Zone administrators may restrict which clients can request AXFR. The RFC recommends that general-purpose implementations support access controls based on IP addresses and TSIG or SIG(0), and should not make open access the default.

An AXFR client MUST use only a fully transferred and checked zone. It stores incoming data first, then makes it available atomically after the transfer succeeds; on error it deletes the partial copy and continues serving the previous version. TSIG or SIG(0) can help verify transfer contents. The RFC says it adds no new security considerations beyond the DNS specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Administrators can limit who receives a full zone copy. A client should switch to new zone data only after the complete transfer passes its checks.
